newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn sees tighter curbs on unemployment benefits.
newsitem.headline: Bonn sees tighter curbs on unemployment benefits.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition believes Germany must toe a hard line on unemployment benefits to meet 1997 budget targets, two key deputies said on Monday.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel already planned to eliminate supplementary federal payments for unemployment benefits, but more steps will be needed, said Adolf Roth and Wolfgang Weng.
The two are respectively parliamentary spokesmen on budgetary matters for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and their junior partners the Free Democrats (FDP).

"An operation like this year's, where the government had to raise an additional 12.5 billion marks ($8.38 billion) for the labour market through a spending freeze and other budget cuts, cannot be repeated," they said.

Job-creation programmes must be sharply cut back, state subsidies for domestic coal mining and other industries must be severely curtailed, and the government must continue to trim its own personnel, they said.
"There is no politically acceptable way to justify less vigilance on spending consolidation or higher borrowing," they said.
Coalition budget experts met with Waigel over the weekend and agreed to cut 1997 spending by 11 billion marks to 440 billion marks and the budget deficit to 56.5 billion marks.
The 1996 deficit, budgeted at 60 billion marks, is now seen at 70 billion marks. The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) say the 1997 deficit will be 18 billion marks larger than budgeted.
Germany and other European nations are under intense pressure to bring their budget deficits down to three percent of economic output in 1997 to qualify for the 1999 start of the single currency.
The government's 1997 budget, approved by the cabinet in July, will get its first reading in parliament this week. The lower house is expected to approve it on Friday.
Unemployment in Germany has hovered near a postwar record four million since the start of the year.
About 250,000 union members rallied across the country over the weekend to protest against the government's savings measures, which they said would aggravate, not relieve, joblessness.
But Chancellery Ministery Friedrich Bohl said he was sure the government's Programme for More Jobs and Growth would have the desired effect.
"That is the whole point," Bohl told German radio on Monday. "We don't just want to save for saving's sake. We want more growth, more employment, more jobs."
